senses: The view that all endeavours are devoid of objective meaning.
The rejection of, or opposition to, religious beliefs, (inherent or objective) moral principles, legal rules, etc., often due to the view that life is meaningless (sense 1).
The rejection of non-proven or non-rationalized assertions in the social and political spheres of society.
A doctrine grounded on the negation of one or more meaningful aspects of life; in particular, the view that nothing in the world actually exists.
Something that is regarded as meaningless.
ety: Probably borrowed from French nihilisme, German Nihilismus, or Late Latin nihilismus; the French, German, and Latin words are derived from Latin nihil (“indefinite nothing”), from nihilum (“nothing”), from ne- (prefix negating the principal meaning) + hīlum (“a trifle; not in the least”). The English word is cognate with Italian nichilismo, Spanish nihilismo, Russian нигили́зм (nigilízm), philosophical doctrine grounded on negation of one or more meaningful aspects of life; emptiness; lack of education and cultural refinement.
examples: Most Christians cannot embrace such radical extremes as the current nihilisms that deny all spiritual and ethical truth. How can a Christian look to Jesus Christ and deny that there is truth? He is the truth.
Although Lexiteers have little patience for the national nihilism of “Davos Man,” the globalist elite, we are no xenophobes.

This mock reasoning proves that those deliberately making use of it are, during the process, insane; inasmuch as they are attempting to reason by means of suppositions, by means of nihilisms, negative quantities.

senses: Having nerve; bold; brazen.
Feeling nervous, anxious or agitated.
ety: From nerve + -y.
examples: It takes a nervy man to promulgate such stuff, and Ted Nelson has made a career out of being nervy.
Blackpool continue to thrive on the adrenalin rush of the end-of-season shoot-out and are heading for a second Wembley date in two years after negotiating a nervy path past Birmingham.

She has been asked on a date to see The Barber of Seville in the company of society’s wealthiest and most eligible bachelor, the Hon Jeremy Malcolm (Ṣọpẹ́ Dìrísù) who is bored by her nervy and untutored chatter.

senses: To rid of lice.
ety: From de- + lice.
examples: Every year, as a fixed ritual just before the spring break, the school held a delicing day.

senses: Absolute; having no exception.
ety: From Late Latin catēgoricus + -al. By surface analysis, category + -ical.
examples: Daytime interests are clearly not such far-reaching psychical sources of dreams as might have been expected from the categorical assertions that everyone continues to carry on his daily business in his dreams.

senses: Resembling or characteristic of a bird.
Having an interest in birds.
Excited due to having encountered a bird or its scent.
ety: From bird + -y.
examples: He was a brisk and birdy little man with a chirping, cheerful voice; and, although he was almost ninety, he always seemed to be in good health and was still immensely active.
It wasn't a childhood influence - I didn't have any ‘birdy’ relatives of neighbours - and neither did I live in the country.
I think your dog is getting birdy.

senses: A women's hairstyle in which the hair is swept upwards from the face and worn high over the forehead.
A men's hairstyle of the 1950s.
A crimson or pink colour.
A corsage with low square neck.
A pattern for silk, with leaves and flowers in pink, blue, and gold.
ety: From French Pompadour, after Madame de Pompadour (1721–1764), mistress of Louis XV.
examples: Squat and perspiring, with a low pompadour and a thin black mustache, he was inevitably disheveled by evening.
The Donald's strange pompadour and Hillary's strange server have eclipsed all the usual primary permutations.

senses: A sauce and marinade for grilled meat originally from Argentina, made from chopped parsley or cilantro, garlic, salt, pepper, onion, and paprika with olive oil.
A traditional pork sandwich with cabbage and salsa, eaten as a snack in the Dominican Republic
ety: Borrowed from Spanish chimichurri, from Basque tximitxurri (literally “a mixture of several things in no particular order”), from Basque immigrants to Argentina and Uruguay in the 19th century. Many folk etymologies also exist.
examples: There are also platters of flavorful pork ribs glazed with smoky chipotle, chicken wings char-grilled with garlicky chimichurri, and plump mussels in green chili tortilla broth with leeks and oven dried tomatoes.

senses: A flower of these plants.
A perfume obtained from this plant or imitating the odour of its flowers.
ety: From French frangipane, from Italian frangipane. Possibly named after Muzio Frangipane, a 16th-century marquess of the Italian noble Frangipani family, who invented a plumeria-scented perfume. The name Frangipane derives from frangere (“to break”) + pane (“bread”), a reference to the family's distribution of bread in time of famine.
examples: The aroma given off by flowers has an aphrodisiac effect, especially on women. This is so particularly in the case of lilies of the valley, gardenia, frangipani, and henna.

I casually let this information drop as our concierge drives us through the resort in a buggy, a frangipani flower tucked behind his ear. He promises to fix the bug problem and drops us off at the lobby.

senses: One who hunts whales; any person employed in the whaling industry.
One who whales (flogs or beats).
Any shark of the family Carcharhinidae; a requiem shark.
ety: From whale + -er. In sense 1, displaced Old English hwælhunta (literally “whale hunter”).
examples: For a whaler's wife to have been “ 'round the Cape” half a dozen times, or even more, was nothing extraordinary.
The whalers brought a new way of life. They brought a chance for travel. Many Chamorros traveled to London and the United States. Over eight hundred Chamorro whalers settled in Honolulu.
The brewing conflict between locals and the whalers prompted then-sheriff Ari Magnússon to draw up a decree that allowed Basques to be killed with impunity in the district.

senses: A confection made from almonds and other nuts, caramelized sugar, and sometimes milk or cream.
ety: Borrowed from French praline.
examples: And so it is with praline, that crunchy, sweet, nut brittle that marries so irresistibly with chocolate.

senses: A traditional French Provençal stewed vegetable dish consisting primarily of tomatoes, zucchini and eggplant.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French ratatouille, from Occitan ratatolha (ratatouille is a dish originally from Nice, and is also found in Provence), French form from diminutive prefix tat- + touiller (“to stir”), from Latin tudiculō (“grind, mix”), from tudes (“hammer”), from Proto-Indo-European *tud-, from *(s)tewd-.
examples: I expected the open-air markets, but defrosted bouillabaisse and canned ratatouille weren’t what I imagined to be staples of Parisian culinary life. Yet they’ve become mainstays.

senses: A curved Nepalese knife used especially by Gurkha fighters; many variants exist, but all share recurve as a common theme.
ety: From Nepali खुकुरी (khukurī).
examples: Soon, however, the bayonets of the 72nd Highlanders and the kukris of the 2nd Gurkhas began to tell.

senses: A place where mead is made.
ety: From mead + -ery. Cognate with Dutch mederij (“meadery”).
examples: People used to come to the Upper Midwest's only dedicated meadery and say, "Huh?" Or perhaps something like, "Oh, yeah, mead, isn't that what Beowulf drank?"

senses: A horn used by hunters.
A simple brass instrument consisting of a horn with no valves, playing only pitches in its harmonic series
The sound of something that bugles.
A sort of wild ox; a buffalo.
examples: Then tooke that squire an horne of bugle small, Which hong adowne his side in twisted gold And tassels gay.

senses: A soft, low-pitched sound; specifically, a soft or sentimental hum, song, or tune.
A continuous hollow low-pitched moan, as of cattle; a bellow.
The low-pitched sound of a large bell.
ety: The verb is borrowed from Scots croon (“to utter a deep, long-drawn-out sound; to utter a lament, mourn; to sing in a wailing voice, whimper, whine; to mutter or sing in an undertone, hum”) [and other forms], from Middle English cronen (“to sing or speak softly, hum, croon”) (croyn (Scotland)) [and other forms], probably from Middle Dutch crônen, krônen (“to groan, moan; to lament”) (modern Dutch kreunen (“to moan”)), or Old High German chrônan, krônen (“to babble, prattle; to chatter”), probably from Proto-West Germanic *kraunijan, from Proto-Indo-European *gerH- (“to cry hoarsely”). The noun
examples: Bitterly she cried as she thought over the old hag's croon:— / "Quick joy, long pain, / You will take your gift again."
From away out in the darkness came a haunting croon from the lubras and children.

senses: A cubbyhole or similar hiding place.
A hug or cuddle.
ety: From Welsh cwtsh (“hug, cuddle; little corner, recess”), from Middle English couche. Doublet of couch.
examples: In front of the pavement again stretched a flat patch of rusty ground, a sort of little platform in the side of the hill where the sagging drying-lines stood and a chickens' cwtch built of orange-boxes.
I am expecting the big man to come round the corner and give me a ‘cwtch’ as he has done beside countless rugby fields.
I don’t mind them coming in for a quick cwtch before trudging back off to their own rooms, as long as no conversation is required and it is literally just a five-minute cuddle.

senses: That emerges, or bursts through; breaking forth.
ety: From Latin ērumpēns, present active participle of ērumpō (“break forth”).
examples: The sun spun aloft, an erumpent orb of balling glory thrilling the blue sky with its brilliance.
He's never looked better on court or on monthly O.N.A.N.T.A. paper. He is erumpent.

senses: The omission of scenes in a film that do not advance the plot.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from Latin ellīpsis, from Ancient Greek ἔλλειψις (élleipsis, “omission”). Doublet of ellipse.
examples: It was now possible for writers and directors to cut scenes that did not further the plot; called "ellipses" by filmmakers.

senses: Japanese chess; a board game similar to chess, invented and traditionally played in Japan.
ety: From Japanese 将棋 (shōgi). Doublet of janggi.
examples: But to the surprise of many in the chess fraternity, Hassabis also began to compete in other mind games: bridge and backgammon, Diplomacy and draughts, as well as the Japanese chess variant shogi.

senses: A gripping listlessness or melancholia caused by boredom; depression.
ety: Unadapted borrowing from French ennui, from Old French enui (“annoyance”), from enuier (modern French ennuyer), from Late Latin inodiō, from Latin in odiō (“hated”). Doublet of annoy.
examples: There have always been individuals who toy with the political extremes out of a sort of high-class ennui.

senses: To make or become hard and stony by impregnating with calcium salts.
To make or become rigid or inflexible; to ossify.
ety: From French calcifier, or from English calcium + -ify.
examples: Over time, the arteries began to calcify.

senses: Having many dots.
ety: From dot + -y.
examples: Look at the dotty pattern on that cheetah's fur.

senses: Capable of being imitated or copied.
Worthy of imitation.
ety: From French imitable, from Latin imitābilis. See imitate.
examples: The characters of man placed in lower stations of life are more usefull, as being imitable by great numbers.

senses: A structure of piled stones, used as a landmark and traditionally constructed by the Inuit, often resembling a humanoid figure.
ety: From Inuktitut ᐃᓄᒃᓱᒃ (inoksok, “in the likeness of a human”).
examples: The Nunavut Territory flag bears a rendering of an inukshuk in the form of a crucifix.

senses: Partaking of, or tending to produce, hallucination.
ety: From hallucinate + -ory.
examples: The painting had a hallucinatory quality, as if it were shifting.
High fever sometimes causes hallucinatory visions.
The film created a hallucinatory atmosphere with its colors and sounds.

senses: The Japanese art of flower arrangement.
An arrangement of flowers according to this art.
ety: From Japanese 生け花 (ikebana, literally “living flowers”).
examples: Along with the island’s 3,000 other Japanese American residents, she celebrated Japanese holidays; learned the art of flower arranging, ikebana; and wore kimonos.

senses: Surly; annoyed; displeased; disgruntled.
ety: 15th century, dialectal, from Middle English chuffe (“a rustic, boor”), in noun sense “stupid fellow”. Adjective sense “surly, displeased” from 1832.
examples: He refused to subscribe, he who had always given so largely to the cause; he was chuff, haughty, overbearing, and seemed bent upon antagonising every prominent suggestion that was made.
Well, I didn't mean with my eyes, Neb; so don't be so chuff on a fellow.

senses: A deep glen or ravine.
ety: Borrowed from Dutch kloof (“ravine”) (South Africa). Doublet of clove (“deep or narrow valley”).
examples: Forming the south boundary of the valley is a range of disrupted bushy hills, with intervening deep and rugged kloofs and ravines, which constituted the retreat of Jan Pockbaas and his rebel banditti.
The grass is rich and matted, you cannot see the soil. It holds the rain and the mist, and they seep into the ground, feeding the streams in every kloof.

Occasionally the narrow dirt road rose above the mist on the slopes of the high round hills, from where one looked down on the silver clouds in the valleys and kloofs below, a magical, incredible sight.

senses: An end or fulfilment of history in general.
ety: Borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔσχατον (éskhaton, “last thing”), from the neuter singular of ἔσχατος (éskhatos, “last”).
examples: He, too, constructs a philosophical history towards an eschaton. In a peculiarly inverted manner he is among the believers in progress—the goal being the undoing of the things done.

The most major of these eschatons involves the 65-million-year Cenozoic era, which began with the Cretaceous-Tertiary extinction event that decimated the dinosaurs and is now closing with another mass extinction event.

From predictions of an imminent technological eschaton to theologically inflected ideas of human perfectibility achieved through technological means, there is ample warrant to see transhumanism as culturally other.

senses: Reptiles and amphibians as a group, especially those of a particular region or time period.
ety: From herpeto- + fauna.
examples: The island is noted for its diverse herpetofauna.
The herpetofaunas of the two regions reflect the differences in their geological histories.

senses: An established phrasal expression whose meaning may not be deducible from the literal meanings of its component words.
An artistic style (for example, in art, architecture, or music); an instance of such a style.
ety: From Middle French idiome, and its source, Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “a peculiarity, property, a peculiar phraseology, idiom”), from ἰδιοῦσθαι (idioûsthai, “to make one's own, appropriate to oneself”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one's own, pertaining to oneself, private, personal, peculiar, separate”). By surface analysis, idi- + -om.
examples: She often spoke in idioms, pining for salad days and complaining about pots calling the kettle black.

senses: A win achieving five han, or three/four han with the required number of fu; worth 12,000 points if the winning player is on the East (dealer) side or 8,000 points otherwise.
ety: Borrowed from Japanese 満貫 (mangan), an orthographic borrowing from Mandarin 滿貫 /满贯 (mǎnguàn).
examples: Even if she gets +8000 points with a mangan, she'll be at -1.
Outside tournaments the chombo penalty is a reverse mangan payment: 4,000 to East, 2,000 to other players.
In mahjong last night I had a six-han hand! I got a mangan.

senses: Of, related to, encountered in, or derived from experience.
ety: From Latin experientiālis, from experientia + -ālis.
examples: Atheists argue that there is no experiential confirmation for the existence of a god.
Each color has a unique experiential quality.
The changes you're talking about here are experiential.

senses: The act of negating something.
A denial or contradiction.
ety: From Middle English negacioun, from Old French negacion, from Latin negātiō (“a denial; negative word”). Morphologically negate + -ion.
examples: As an isolating language Belter Creole is rich in particles. Particles are used to indicate both negation and interrogation: na is the negative particle and it is placed before the verb
But it pleased her to play on my passion / And whet me to pleadings / That won from her mirthful negations / And scornings undue.

senses: Combining disparate elements in one system, especially as in forms of religious observance, philosophical systems, or artistic creations.
ety: Back-formation from syncretism: by surface analysis, syncret(ize) + -ic.
examples: To cite another obvious case, there can be few things more syncretic than Roman Catholic canon law, where the doctrine of a Galilean peasant was built into Roman imperial legality.

senses: Not straight; wavy and irregular.
ety: From squiggle + -y.
examples: She didn't have a ruler, so she drew a squiggly line to highlight the main points.
My first memories of eating are bowls of squiggly pasta with red sauce and lots of white cheese.

senses: A toy for children, comprising an artificial (usually plastic) stem and a flower that spins round in the wind like a tiny windmill.
A firework that spins in the shape of a spinning wheel.
A pastry made by laying out dough flat, smearing a topping over it and rolling it up into a spiral, then baking it, resulting in a swirl of filling.
Any food product consisting of layers (for example of pastry and sweet filling, or of bread and meat) rolled into a spiral.
ety: From pin + wheel.
examples: The sun blazing late in the afternoon, this long hilarious day like a pinwheel inexhaustibly throwing off sparks.

senses: Hot and humid; sweltering.
Emitting great heat.
Sexually enthralling.
ety: From sulter (“verb (obsolete), a variant of swelter”) + -y; compare sweltry.
examples: The detachment of Tancred, fifty spears and their armed retinue, which amounted fully to five hundred men, after having taken a short and hasty refreshment, were in arms and mounted before the sultry hour of noon.
The heat had been painfully oppressive all day; and it was now a close and sultry night.
The battlefield—an undulating, parched, and dusty expanse—is lying under the sultry sun of a July afternoon.

senses: An area of land that has been cleared by cutting the vegetation and burning it; slash and burn.
ety: Possibly from a dialectal form *swiden of Middle English swithen, past participle of Middle English swithen (“to burn, scorch, singe”), from Old Norse svíða (“to singe, burn”). Compare also Old Norse sviðinn (“burnt, singed”, past participle). Alternatively, from Old Norse sviðna (“to be burned”) or Old High German swedan (“to be burned”). Either way, probably ultimately from Proto-Germanic *swīþaną. First attested in 1868. If their respective theories align, then a distant cognate of German Schwyz, hence Swiss.
examples: Kamiali Village is a community of swidden horticulturists and fishers lying 80 kilometers in a south-southeasterly direction along the coast from the City of Lae, Papua New Guinea.
These facts reinforced the view that the Maya drew their basic sustenance from corn, most of it grown on slash-and-burn plots known as swiddens.

senses: Synonym of ferrochromium.
ety: From ferro- + chrome.
examples: The capital raising has been forced by plummeting ferrochrome prices which slumped after Chinese mills cut 55 per cent from the price of the alloy used to make stainless steel.
